questions.q: In a star network, how is each device connected?
options: By its own cable to a central switch
To the two devices either side of it
To every other device on the network
By a single cable that every device shares
questions.feedback: Its own cable to the centre. That is why one failing cable affects one device.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 6 — Star and mesh networks, station 1: Star topology

questions.q: Explain one advantage of a star network over a network where all devices share one cable.

markPoints.concept: each device has its own connection to the switch
accept: own cable|own connection|own line|separate cable|separate line|separate connection|individual|its own|dedicated
markPoints.exemplar: Each device has its own cable to the switch.

markPoints.concept: so one cable failing affects only that device, and there are no collisions
accept: only that|just that|one device|rest keep working|others continue|no collision|collisions|does not affect
markPoints.exemplar: So if one cable fails only that device is affected and the rest keep working.

questions.example: In a star network each device has its own cable to the central switch, so if one cable fails only that one device drops off and everybody else carries on working.
questions.paraphrase: Every machine runs a separate line to the switch, which means a broken cable only takes out the computer at the end of it.
questions.feedback: Own cable, therefore isolated failure. Either consequence — one device affected, or no collisions — earns the second mark.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 6 — Star and mesh networks, station 1: Star topology

questions.q: What is the main disadvantage of a star network?
options: If the central switch fails, the whole network goes down
Data has to pass through every other device first
Only one device can send data at a time
Every device needs to know every other device's address
questions.feedback: The centre is a single point of failure. That is the price of the convenience.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 6 — Star and mesh networks, station 1: Star topology

questions.q: State what is meant by a full mesh network.

markPoints.concept: every device is connected directly to every other device
markPoints.exemplar: Every device is connected directly to every other device.

questions.example: A network in which every device is connected directly to every other device.
questions.paraphrase: All the machines are linked to all of the others.
questions.feedback: Every device to every other. A partial mesh has some of those connections but not all.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 6 — Star and mesh networks, station 6: Full mesh

questions.q: Explain why a mesh network is more reliable than a star network.

markPoints.concept: there is more than one route between any two devices
accept: more than one route|more than one path|several routes|several paths|many routes|another route|another path|multiple paths|different paths|alternative|other path|different route|reroute|redirect
markPoints.exemplar: There is more than one route between any two devices.

markPoints.concept: so if one connection fails the data can take a different path
markPoints.exemplar: So if one connection fails the data simply takes another route.

questions.example: In a mesh there is more than one route between any two devices, so if a connection fails the data can be sent by a different path, whereas in a star everything depends on the one switch in the middle.
questions.paraphrase: Because several different paths link each pair of devices, a broken link just means the traffic goes round another way.
questions.feedback: More than one route, therefore a failure is survivable.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 6 — Star and mesh networks, station 6: Full mesh

questions.q: The internet is an example of a full mesh network.
questions.feedback: False. It is a partial mesh: there are many alternative routes, but no computer is connected directly to every other one.
questions.misconception: A full mesh of the internet would need an impossible number of connections.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 6 — Star and mesh networks, station 6: Full mesh

questions.q: A full mesh network of 50 computers is rarely built. Explain why.

markPoints.concept: the number of connections needed is enormous
markPoints.exemplar: The number of cables needed is enormous.

markPoints.concept: which makes it very expensive and difficult to install
markPoints.exemplar: This makes it far too expensive and difficult to install.

questions.example: Every computer would need a direct connection to all 49 others, which is well over a thousand cables in total, so the cost of the cable and the difficulty of installing it make a full mesh impractical at that size.
questions.paraphrase: Each machine would have to be wired to all the rest, running to more than a thousand links, which is far too costly and awkward to put in.
questions.feedback: The number of connections grows very fast, and the cost and difficulty grow with it.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 6 — Star and mesh networks, station 6: Full mesh

questions.q: In a full mesh network of 6 computers, how many connections are needed?
questions.feedback: Each of the 6 connects to 5 others, and each cable is counted twice, so (6 × 5) ÷ 2 = 15.
questions.hint: How many does each computer need, and how many times is each cable counted?
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 6 — Star and mesh networks, station 6: Full mesh
